The post Meet Facebook’s Your Algorithm: How Meta Turns Plain-Language Preferences Into Ranking appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta has published an engineering deep dive on Facebook Your Algorithm . Your Algorithm lets people tell Facebook, in plain language, what they want in Feed and Reels. Meta announced the feature on October 13, 2026. The new post shows how large language models (LLMs) sit inside a production recommender. For developers, it is a rare look at explicit preferences wired into an implicit-signal ranking stack. TL;DR What: ‘ Your algorithm is an end-to-end system that addresses the limitations of adaptability and nuance in recommendations’ Runs on: Meta’s server-side ranking stack, plus on-device cache invalidation in the Facebook app. Best: Explicit interests feed 4 retrieval sources and apply across both Feed and Reels. Bottom line: Best: a clear blueprint for LLM-steered ranking What is Facebook Your Algorithm? Your Algorithm is an AI-powered preference page for Facebook Feed and Reels. It has 3 parts, per Meta’s engineering post . A one-sentence “Lately Summary” describes recent viewing. An “Interested In” list is prefilled from past activity. A “Not Interested In” list holds exclusions. Users can type interests, move them between lists, or delete them. Access is through the three-dot menu on posts, according to Meta’s newsroom . Meta’s framing is simple. Implicit engagement signals scale well but adapt slowly and miss nuance. Explicit, stated preferences close that gap. How does the Your Algorithm system work? Meta splits the preference lifecycle into 4 components: Profile generation: An LLM turns regularly refreshed interest signals into readable topic names. It also writes the Lately Summary. Preference management: An LLM checks that a typed phrase is a coherent topic. It detects duplicates and maps the phrase to a clean topic name. This step runs on a smaller, cheaper model. Ranking: Both lists are applied across the ranking funnel. Delivery optimization: Changes reach the feed faster. Validated interests are enriched with an embedding and search keywords. They are saved to a shared store that both Feed and Reels read. A separate component runs integrity and safety checks. How do “Interested In” topics reach the feed? Each interest drives 4 retrieval sources. 2 match content directly: search and clusters of closely related topics. 2 extend reach: the content graph and item-to-item similarity. A relevance check compares the interest’s meaning with each candidate. Passing candidates get a late-stage ranking promotion. A reranking control layer then stops flooding: Repeats of the same interest are spaced out. Each interest’s daily contribution is capped. Retrieval fetches for 1 interest per request. New interests get temporary extra weight. How does “Not Interested In” filtering work? Meta calls this layered filtering at every stage. Ranking uses embedding comparison to remove close matches. Demotion rules push down near matches. A fine-tuned LLM reranker then reviews the final list. Quality requests, such as less AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, take a different path. They map to dedicated demotion signals, not topic matching. Requests naming a creator filter that creator directly. On the client, cache invalidation removes queued items that match a new exclusion before display. Why use a small fine-tuned LLM as the reranker? The reranker is trained to return only the items to remove. Meta says this small fine-tuned model beat a general-purpose model judging each item. It was faster and more reliable. Outputting a short removal list is cheaper than scoring every candidate. Speed comes from a “supplementary tail load.” Adding an interest fires an extra fetch outside the normal cycle. Meta gives no latency figure for it.
